theme.q:
Consider these two situations.
I. A translator works through a document line by line, putting one line into French and the next into Spanish, and so on.
II. A Dutch tourist in London has to stop herself from looking left first before crossing the street.
Which executive functions do these situations mainly call on?
o: I calls on shifting, II calls on inhibition
I calls on updating, II calls on inhibition
I calls on shifting, II calls on updating
I calls on inhibition, II calls on shifting
theme.spot: Switching back and forth between two tasks, or stopping a habit?
theme.why: Alternating between two tasks (French, Spanish, French...) is shifting. Holding back a strong, automatic response (looking left, as at home) is inhibition, the function behind the Stroop task. Updating would be replacing old contents of working memory with the newest item, which neither situation is about.
theme.src: [CORE][LO B4][IDQ B5] Miyake et al. (2000); E&K pp. 220-221

theme.q: Taxi drivers judged which of two routes through their city was shorter. They did this while either repeating ‘the the the’ out loud or pressing the keys of a keypad in a fixed clockwise order. Only the keypad task slowed their judgements. This pattern indicates that
o: the phonological loop is involved in judging routes, but the visuo-spatial sketchpad isn’t
the visuo-spatial sketchpad is involved in judging routes, but the phonological loop isn’t
the central executive is involved in judging routes, but the visuo-spatial sketchpad isn’t
the episodic buffer is involved in judging routes, but the phonological loop isn’t
theme.spot: Which component does each second task load, and which one hurt?
theme.why: Repeating ‘the the the’ is articulatory suppression: it occupies the phonological loop, and it did not hurt, so the loop is not needed. Pressing keys in a fixed spatial pattern loads the visuo-spatial sketchpad (the same task Robbins et al. used), and it did hurt. Two tasks only clash when they use the same component.
theme.src: [CORE][LO B5][IDQ B1] dual-task logic; Robbins et al. (1996), E&K p. 216

theme.q: Two memory tasks (1 and 2) are each combined with two interference tasks (A and B). Which pattern of results gives the strongest evidence that tasks 1 and 2 rely on separate working memory components?
o: Both tasks get worse when they are done at the same time than when each is done alone
Both tasks are disrupted to a similar degree by random number generation
A disrupts task 1 but not task 2; B disrupts task 2 but not task 1
A disrupts task 1, and it disrupts task 2 even more strongly than task 1
theme.spot: Look for the crossover: each interference task hurts only ‘its own’ task.
theme.why: A crossover (double dissociation) shows that each task has its own resource: A only hurts task 1, B only hurts task 2. If one interference task were simply harder, it would hurt both tasks, as in the last option. Equal disruption by random number generation points to the shared central executive, not to separate components.
theme.src: [LO B5][IDQ B3] Klauer & Zhao (2004); E&K pp. 215-219

theme.q: In the maxispan procedure, participants rehearse aloud only the first letters of a list (shown in blue) and keep the remaining black letters in mind without rehearsing them. The figure shows recall of the black letters as a function of how many blue letters had to be rehearsed. What would the figure look like if the phonological loop could comfortably hold six items?

chart.title: Maxispan: recall of the non-rehearsed (black) letters
chart.note: Approximate values read from Barrouillet et al., Experiment 1.

o: The bar for 5 blue letters would be about as high as the bars for 3 and 4
All three bars would be lower than they are now
The bar for 3 blue letters would be the lowest of the three
The bar for 4 blue letters would drop to about the level of the bar for 5 blue letters
theme.spot: ‘What would it look like if...’: find where the drop is now, and ask whether it would still happen.
theme.why: Recall of the black letters now drops only at 5 rehearsed letters: the loop overflows and rehearsal starts to cost the other letters. If the loop could hold six, five letters would still fit, so the 5 bar would stay level with 3 and 4. The drop at 5 is why the conclusion is that the loop holds about four items.
theme.src: [CORE] Barrouillet et al. maxispan, Experiment 1 (practice exam figure); pty_t2 2.14.2

theme.q: Participants kept either dot locations (spatial task) or Chinese characters (visual task) in mind while doing a movement discrimination or a colour discrimination task. The figure shows how much each secondary task disrupted each main task. Which statement is NOT supported by the figure?

chart.title: Interference with each main task
chart.note: Approximate values from Eysenck & Keane Figure 6.6 (Klauer & Zhao, 2004).

o: Colour discrimination hardly disrupted memory for the locations of the dots
Movement discrimination disrupted the spatial task more than the visual task
Movement discrimination disrupted the visual task more than colour discrimination did
Colour discrimination disrupted the visual task much more than it disrupted the spatial task
theme.spot: ‘NOT supported’: check each sentence against the bars, one pair at a time.
theme.why: For the Chinese characters (visual task), colour discrimination caused about 9.4% interference and movement discrimination only about 4.2%, so the third statement is false. The other three match the figure: colour barely touched the dots (about -1.2%), movement hurt dots (6.3%) more than characters (4.2%), and colour hurt characters more than dots. This crossover is Klauer and Zhao's evidence for a separate visual and spatial component.
theme.src: [LO B5][IDQ B3] Klauer & Zhao (2004), E&K Figure 6.6 (approximate values)

theme.q: Which of these statements about the working memory model is NOT correct?
o: The visual cache stores information about visual form and colour
The central executive is a modality-free system with limited capacity
The episodic buffer can hold about four chunks of integrated information
The phonological store actively rehearses words to keep them available
theme.spot: Store or process? The store is the ‘inner ear’, the rehearsal is the ‘inner voice’.
theme.why: The phonological store is passive: it holds speech sounds that fade within about two seconds. Rehearsal is done by the separate articulatory control process (the inner voice). The other statements are correct descriptions of the visual cache, the central executive and the episodic buffer (Baddeley, 2012).
theme.src: [CORE][LO B2][LO B3] E&K pp. 215-218; Baddeley (1990, 2012)

theme.q: A quizmaster reads out 15 song titles. Group A writes down as many titles as they can straight away. Group B first spends 30 seconds solving sums out loud and then writes down the titles. Compared with group A, group B will recall
o: fewer of the first titles, but about as many of the last titles
fewer titles from every position, to the same degree
fewer of the last titles, but about as many of the first titles
more of the titles from the middle of the list
theme.spot: A filled delay before recall: which items were only in short-term memory?
theme.why: The last titles are still in short-term memory at the end of the list. Thirty seconds of sums push them out, so the recency effect disappears. The first titles were rehearsed more and reached long-term memory, so the primacy effect survives the delay.
theme.src: [CORE][LO A2][LO A5][IDQ A2] serial-position effect; M&F pp. 113-114

theme.q: According to Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968), how does information get into long-term memory?
o: Directly from sensory memory, whenever attention is low
Through the episodic buffer, which binds features into chunks
Through the central executive, which holds it briefly before passing it on
Through rehearsal of the information while it is in short-term memory
theme.spot: Atkinson-Shiffrin = boxes in a row; what moves information from box 2 to box 3?
theme.why: In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, information passes step by step from sensory memory to short-term memory, and rehearsal (a control process people actively use) transfers it to long-term memory. That is also how the model explains the primacy effect: early items get the most rehearsal. The episodic buffer and central executive belong to Baddeley's later working memory model.
theme.src: [CORE][LO A5][IDQ A4] M&F p. 117; Atkinson & Shiffrin (1968)

theme.q: A student has to keep the string N L B B C U S A E U in mind for a few seconds. She finds this hard until she notices that it reads NL, BBC, USA, EU. After that it is easy. Which explanation fits best?
o: She turned ten letters into four chunks, which fits easily in short-term memory
She released herself from proactive interference by switching to a new category
She moved the letters from the phonological loop into the visual cache
She enlarged her short-term memory capacity from about seven to about ten letters
theme.spot: Same letters, fewer units: what is the unit of short-term memory?
theme.why: Short-term memory capacity is counted in chunks, not letters (Miller, 1956). Familiar abbreviations from long-term memory pack ten letters into four chunks, well within the limit. The capacity itself does not grow; each slot simply holds more. Release from proactive interference is about a change of meaning category across trials, which does not happen here.
theme.src: [CORE][LO A1][LO A4][IDQ A1] Miller (1956); M&F pp. 111-112

theme.q: In Peterson and Peterson's (1959) study, participants saw three letters such as CHJ and recalled them after a delay. What did they do during the delay, and why?
o: They repeated ‘the the the’, to block the phonological store
They counted backwards by threes, to prevent them from rehearsing the letters
They tapped a spatial pattern, to keep the sketchpad busy
They read new letters aloud, in order to create retroactive interference on purpose
theme.spot: What kept the letters from being repeated silently?
theme.why: Participants counted backwards by threes from a three-digit number. This distracting task prevents rehearsal, so the study shows how fast unrehearsed information is lost: after only about 5 seconds, roughly half the letters were forgotten (after many earlier trials). Articulatory suppression and spatial tapping are later dual-task methods from the working memory literature.
theme.src: [LO A2][LO A3][IDQ A3] Brown/Peterson and Peterson technique; M&F p. 113

theme.q: Two groups do four Brown/Peterson trials, each with three words and 18 seconds of counting backwards. Group 1 sees vegetables on trials 1 to 3, group 2 sees musical instruments. On trial 4 both groups see three fruits. What do you expect on trial 4?
o: Both groups recall about equally poorly, because interference builds up over any three trials
Group 1 recalls more, because vegetables prime the related fruit words
Group 2 recalls more, because instruments are less similar in meaning to fruits
Group 2 recalls less, because a change of category confuses participants
theme.spot: How similar in meaning is the old category to the new one?
theme.why: Proactive interference depends on semantic similarity: earlier words block new words that are similar in meaning. Vegetables, like fruits, are edible plants, so interference stays high. Instruments share nothing with fruits, so group 2 shows release from proactive interference (as the occupations group did in Wickens et al., 1976).
theme.src: [LO A3][IDQ A5] Wickens et al. (1976); M&F pp. 115-117

theme.q:
Judge these statements about the Brown/Peterson task.
I. Letters from earlier trials make the letters on a later trial harder to recall.
II. The counting task during the delay can itself interfere with memory for the letters.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
theme.spot: Two directions of interference: from old to new, and from new to old.
theme.why: Statement I describes proactive interference: earlier trials hurt later ones, which is why recall falls after the first few trials. Statement II describes retroactive interference: the new material processed during the delay (the counting) disturbs what was learned just before. Both play a part in the fast forgetting the task shows.
theme.src: [LO A2][IDQ A3][IDQ A5] M&F pp. 113-116

theme.q: In Logie's (1995) account of the visuo-spatial sketchpad, which job belongs to the inner scribe?
o: Storing the visual form and colour of objects
Rehearsing speech-based information silently
Binding information from different senses into chunks
Processing spatial and movement information
theme.spot: Cache = what it looks like. Scribe = where it is and how it moves.
theme.why: The inner scribe handles spatial and movement information; it also rehearses the contents of the visual cache and passes information to the central executive. The visual cache stores form and colour. Silent rehearsal of speech is the phonological loop, and binding into chunks is the episodic buffer.
theme.src: [CORE][LO B3] Logie (1995); E&K p. 218

theme.q:
Vergauwe et al. (2009) repeated Klauer and Zhao's visual and spatial interference design with more demanding interference tasks. Judge these statements.
I. Their results show that the visual and spatial parts of the sketchpad are a single system.
II. Interference that is specific to the visual or spatial component appears mainly when the interference tasks need little attention.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
theme.spot: Did the demanding tasks remove the split, or hide it behind something general?
theme.why: With demanding tasks, each type of interference hurt both main tasks about equally, because both now drew on the central executive's general attention. That hides the split rather than removing it, so statement I is false. Specific interference shows up with undemanding tasks, so statement II is true: the separation of the components depends on attention.
theme.src: [LO B5][IDQ B4] Vergauwe et al. (2009); E&K p. 219

theme.q: Weaker and stronger chess players chose moves while doing one of four secondary tasks. The figure shows the quality of the moves. What would the figure look like if choosing chess moves relied mainly on the phonological loop?

chart.title: Quality of chess-move selection
chart.note: Approximate values from Eysenck & Keane Figure 6.4 (Robbins et al., 1996).

o: Move quality would also drop under articulatory suppression
Move quality would drop under the tapping control task
Only the weaker players would be affected by the keypad task
Move quality would rise under random number generation
theme.spot: Which secondary task loads the loop, and what does it do now?
theme.why: Articulatory suppression (saying ‘see-saw’) occupies the phonological loop. In the real data it left move quality almost unchanged, while the keypad task (sketchpad) and random number generation (central executive) lowered it. If the loop were needed, the suppression bars would drop too. Tapping is the control task that loads no specific component.
theme.src: [CORE][IDQ B1] Robbins et al. (1996), E&K Figure 6.4 (approximate values)

theme.q: Which finding is evidence for the phonological store, rather than for the articulatory rehearsal process?
o: Memory span is larger for short words than for long words
Articulatory suppression removes the word-length effect for written words
Similar-sounding words are harder to recall in the correct order
A patient who cannot rehearse verbally shows no word-length effect
theme.spot: Similarity effect or word-length effect: which one points to storage of sounds?
theme.why: The phonological similarity effect (FEE, HE, KNEE are recalled worse in order than BAY, HOE, IT) shows that the store keeps a sound-based code, so similar sounds blur. The other three options are all about the word-length effect, which reflects the time needed for rehearsal by the inner voice.
theme.src: [LO B3][IDQ B2] Larsen et al. (2000); Baddeley et al. (1975); Jacquemot et al. (2011); E&K pp. 217-218

theme.q: Patient PV had a digit span of only two items, yet ran a shop and raised a family. What did Baddeley et al. (1998) find when she tried to learn new material?
o: She learned pairs of Italian words normally, but learned no Russian words over ten trials
She could not learn pairs of Italian words, but learned Russian words with practice
She learned both kinds of pairs normally, which shows the loop has no everyday function at all
She learned neither kind of pair, because her long-term memory was also damaged
theme.spot: What is the loop for in daily life?
theme.why: PV, a native Italian speaker, learned pairs of familiar Italian words normally but learned no Russian words (with Italian translations) over ten trials. So damage to the phonological loop gives a selective deficit, and the loop matters most for learning new vocabulary. Papagno et al. (1991) found the same in healthy people under articulatory suppression.
theme.src: [LO B3][CORE] Baddeley et al. (1988, 1998); E&K p. 218

theme.q: How does Baddeley (2012) now describe the relation between the episodic buffer and the central executive?
o: The executive must actively bind all features before they can enter the buffer
Integrated information can be held in the buffer without direct executive involvement
The buffer takes over the executive's work when a task becomes demanding
The buffer stores the executive's plans, because the executive itself cannot store anything
theme.spot: Allen et al. (2012): did counting backwards stop the binding?
theme.why: Baddeley (2000) first assumed the executive controls access to the buffer. Later findings changed this: counting backwards hurt memory for colour-shape combinations no more than for single features (Allen et al., 2012), so binding happens automatically elsewhere. The buffer is now an essentially passive structure on which these bindings are displayed. The last option is tempting because the executive indeed stores nothing, but the buffer does not hold its plans.
theme.src: [CORE][LO B1][IDQ B6] Baddeley (2012); Allen et al. (2012); E&K pp. 225-226

theme.q:
McGonnell et al. (2024) entered age (step 1), then phonological processing and attention problems (step 2), then the four working memory components (step 3). Only the visuospatial sketchpad added unique variance to calculation. The table shows how each component correlated with phonological processing.
Working memory componentr with phonological processing
Phonological loop.62
Verbal central executive.59
Visuospatial central executive.42
Visuospatial sketchpad.30
Which conclusion fits the table best?
o: The sketchpad had the highest correlation with calculation of all four components
The loop and verbal executive were unrelated to calculation in this sample
The sketchpad shared least with a step-2 predictor, so more of its link was new
Phonological processing was measured with the AWMA, which favours verbal components
theme.spot: A predictor only adds unique variance for the part that was not explained by earlier steps.
theme.why: The verbal components share a lot with phonological processing (.62 and .59), which was already in the model from step 2. Their link with calculation was therefore largely explained already. The sketchpad shared least (.30), so its link with calculation was more unique. In fact the sketchpad had the lowest correlation with calculation (.42; the loop had .53), and all four components did correlate with it.
theme.src: [LO C3][IDQ C2] McGonnell et al. (2024) Table 2 and Table 3

theme.q: The AWMA, used by McGonnell et al. (2024), crosses type of material (verbal or visuospatial) with type of demand (only holding, or holding plus processing). Which pair of subtests differs ONLY in the type of demand?
o: Digit recall and dot matrix
Word recall and block recall
Digit recall and backwards digits
Listening recall and spatial span
theme.spot: Same material, but one adds a job on top of remembering.
theme.why: Digit recall (just repeat the digits) and backwards digit recall (repeat them in reverse) both use verbal material, but the second adds processing, so it measures the verbal central executive rather than the phonological loop. The other three pairs keep the demand the same but differ in material (verbal vs visuospatial); listening recall and spatial span, for example, are both executive tasks.
theme.src: [LO C1][LO C2][IDQ C1] McGonnell et al. (2024), AWMA

theme.q:
Judge these statements about the regression results of McGonnell et al. (2024).
I. As the authors predicted, both visuospatial working memory components added unique variance to calculation.
II. Attention problems were no longer a significant predictor once the visuospatial sketchpad was added.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
theme.spot: Prediction vs outcome: which visuospatial component made it?
theme.why: The authors predicted that both visuospatial components would add unique variance, but only the sketchpad did (10.2%), not the visuospatial central executive, so I is false. With the sketchpad in step 3, attention problems dropped out (p = .23), so II is true. Phonological processing stayed significant.
theme.src: [LO C3][IDQ C2] McGonnell et al. (2024), results and discussion

theme.q: A school psychologist assesses a nine-year-old who struggles with written sums. Following McGonnell et al. (2024), what should the assessment include?
o: Only a parent rating of attention, since attention is the core deficit in math difficulty
Tests of visuospatial skills and working memory, alongside the child's math skills
Only verbal tests, since most math instruction is given in words
Only an IQ test, since IQ was the first predictor in their regression
theme.spot: What do the authors recommend for assessments of math difficulty?
theme.why: The authors conclude that visuospatial skills and working memory should be part of assessments for math difficulty, because strengths and weaknesses there help explain the problem and plan remediation. Attention lost its significance once the sketchpad was in the model, so it is not the core deficit. IQ was deliberately not entered as a predictor; age was step 1.
theme.src: [LO C4][IDQ C4] McGonnell et al. (2024), section 5.5

theme.q: Combining their results with earlier work, McGonnell et al. (2024) suggest that working memory components matter at different ages. In which order do they become especially important for math?
o: Visuospatial sketchpad first, then phonological loop, then central executive
Central executive first, then phonological loop, then visuospatial sketchpad
Phonological loop first, then central executive, then visuospatial sketchpad
Phonological loop first, then visuospatial sketchpad, then central executive
theme.spot: Early teaching is spoken; complex math comes last.
theme.why: At age seven the phonological loop predicted math best, at eight the sketchpad (Alloway & Passolunghi, 2011). McGonnell et al. add that the central executive becomes important later, as math becomes more complex. This fits how teaching develops: early instruction and feedback are mostly verbal.
theme.src: [LO C3][IDQ C3] McGonnell et al. (2024) discussion; Alloway & Passolunghi (2011)

theme.q: According to the unitary-store view, short-term memory is simply the part of long-term memory that is active at the moment. Which finding is hardest for this view to explain?
o: Familiar abbreviations such as BBC make a letter string easier to hold
Patients with wider medial temporal lobe damage were impaired on short-term memory for faces
Learning word pairs held only briefly was not linked to hippocampal activation
Words from a familiar category are easier to recall than unrelated letters
theme.spot: Unitary view predicts: STM uses the same brain areas as LTM.
theme.why: If STM were only activated LTM, the hippocampus (central for LTM) should also support STM. Bergmann et al. (2012) found no hippocampal activation for word pairs held in STM but later lost from LTM. Race et al.'s face results support the unitary view in part, and the effects of familiar knowledge fit it well, because long-term knowledge does shape what STM holds.
theme.src: [LO B1][CORE] Bergmann et al. (2012); Race et al. (2013); E&K p. 214

theme.q: The figure shows two free-recall curves for the same 15-word list. Which change in procedure most likely produced curve B?

chart.title: Free recall by serial position (illustrative)
chart.note: Illustrative data showing the typical pattern (after Rundus, 1971).

o: The words were presented at a faster rate
Recall was delayed by 30 seconds of counting backwards
All words in the list came from one and the same semantic category
Recall started immediately after the last word
theme.spot: Which end of the curve changed, and what removes that end?
theme.why: Curve B has the same primacy effect as curve A but no recency effect. The last words are only in short-term memory, and a distracting task before recall pushes them out. A faster presentation rate would lower the start of the curve (less rehearsal, less primacy), and immediate recall is what produced the recency in curve A.
theme.src: [CORE][LO A2][LO A5][IDQ A5] serial-position effect; M&F pp. 113-114

m1.q: Participants hear a long list of words from several categories (animals, colours, countries) and must always be able to report the most recent word from each category. Which executive function does this task mainly measure?
o: Inhibition
Shifting
Updating
Task setting
m1.spot: Keep replacing old contents with the newest item.
m1.why: Updating is monitoring working memory and quickly adding new items and deleting old ones, as in keeping track of the latest member of each category (Miyake et al., 2000). Inhibition is overriding a dominant response, shifting is switching between tasks. Task setting is one of Stuss and Alexander's processes: planning, setting up a stimulus-response relationship.
m1.src: [CORE][LO B4] Miyake et al. (2000); E&K p. 221

m1.q: In the maxispan procedure, participants rehearsed 3, 4 or 5 letters aloud and kept the other letters in mind without rehearsal. The figure shows recall of the non-rehearsed letters. Which conclusion can be drawn?

chart.title: Recall of non-rehearsed letters in maxispan
chart.note: Approximate values read from Barrouillet et al., Experiment 1.

o: Rehearsing letters aloud never affects memory for the other letters
The episodic buffer can hold about five rehearsed letters
Rehearsing five letters overloads the loop, which suggests it holds about four
The more letters are rehearsed aloud, the better the other letters are recalled
m1.why: Recall of the non-rehearsed letters stays about the same with 3 or 4 rehearsed letters and drops with 5. So up to four letters fit in the phonological loop; with five, rehearsal overflows and takes resources from the other letters. The study is about the loop, not the episodic buffer.
m1.src: [CORE] Barrouillet et al. maxispan, Experiment 1 (practice exam figure)

m1.q: Which of these statements about the Atkinson-Shiffrin model is NOT correct?
o: Information passes through separate stores one step at a time
People actively control the flow of information, for example by rehearsing it
Short-term memory both stores information and carries out complex processing
The model compares the mind with the operations of a computer
m1.spot: Storage-only box, or storage plus processing? Which model added processing?
m1.why: In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, short-term memory is a storage box on the way to long-term memory. The idea that it also does complex processing came with Baddeley and Hitch's working memory, and it is one of that model's advantages. The other three statements describe Atkinson and Shiffrin's information-processing approach correctly.

m1.q: McGonnell et al. (2024) found that the visuospatial sketchpad predicts children's calculation skills. Which study design would be needed to find out whether the sketchpad helps children acquire these skills?
o: Testing the same children's sketchpad and calculation repeatedly over several school years
Adding IQ as an extra predictor in the first step of the regression
Testing a larger sample of children of one age group at a single moment
Replacing the parent ratings of attention with a computer task of attention
m1.spot: What kind of design did the authors say they lacked?
m1.why: The study measured everything at one moment, so it shows a relationship, not what develops first or causes what. The authors call for a longitudinal design, following the same children over time. The other changes would improve the study, but they still give a single snapshot.
m1.src: [LO C4][IDQ C4] McGonnell et al. (2024), sections 5.5 and 5.6

m2.q: Participants listened to spoken shopping lists and recalled them in order. While listening they either pressed keys in a fixed spatial pattern or kept saying ‘hiya’ out loud. Only saying ‘hiya’ harmed recall. What does this show?
o: The lists were held in the visuo-spatial sketchpad
The lists were held in the phonological loop
The lists were held in the central executive
The lists were held in the visual cache
m2.spot: Which second task hurt, and which component does it load?
m2.why: Saying ‘hiya’ over and over is articulatory suppression, which occupies the phonological loop. It hurt recall, so the lists were held there. Pressing keys in a spatial pattern loads the sketchpad, and it did not hurt. The central executive does not store information at all.

m2.q: In the morning your partner reads out a list of 12 groceries. Twenty minutes later, at the shop, which items are you most likely to have forgotten?
o: Only the items at the end of the list
Only the items at the beginning of the list
The items in the middle and at the end of the list
Only the items in the middle of the list, not those at the ends
m2.spot: After a long delay, which part of the U-curve is gone?
m2.why: Twenty minutes of other activity empties short-term memory, so the recency advantage for the last items is lost. The first items received more rehearsal and reached long-term memory (primacy), so they survive. The middle items were never well remembered, so they are forgotten as well.
m2.src: [CORE][LO A2][IDQ A2] serial-position effect; M&F p. 114

m2.q: Which statement about the central executive is correct?
o: It briefly stores the intermediate results of mental arithmetic, such as 80 in 27 × 4
It depends only on the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex
Researchers agree that it consists of exactly three functions
Executive problems can also occur in patients with little or no frontal damage
m2.spot: Boss who stores nothing; where in the brain, and how many functions?
m2.why: Executive processes are linked mainly to prefrontal cortex, but patients with diffuse trauma or multiple sclerosis can have poor executive functioning with little or no frontal damage (Stuss, 2011). The executive stores nothing: intermediate results are held by the other components. The number and nature of executive processes is still disputed.

m2.q: McGonnell et al. (2024) predicted that both visuospatial components would predict calculation, but only the visuospatial sketchpad did. Which explanation did they offer?
o: The visuospatial central executive was not measured by the AWMA
Children with ADHD had a weaker visuospatial central executive
The two visuospatial components cannot be reliably separated from each other
The sketchpad subtests were easier, so they gave more reliable scores
m2.spot: Two components that overlap so much that they compete for the same variance.
m2.why: Miyake et al. (2001) showed that the visuospatial sketchpad and the visuospatial central executive cannot be reliably separated, because both relate equally to executive functioning. So math may be linked to visuospatial memory in broad terms. The visuospatial executive was measured by the AWMA (for example odd-one-out and Mister X).

m3.q:
Participants held either a list of letters or a set of positions in mind, while doing either articulatory suppression or spatial tapping. The table shows the percentage of errors (illustrative data).
Articulatory suppressionSpatial tapping
Letters32%11%
Positions12%30%
What can be concluded?
o: Positions are held in the phonological loop, letters in the sketchpad
Both tasks depend mainly on the central executive
Letters are held in the phonological loop, positions in the sketchpad
Spatial tapping is simply more difficult than articulatory suppression
m3.spot: Which interference hurts which memory task: is there a crossover?
m3.why: Articulatory suppression hurts the letters most, so they are in the phonological loop. Spatial tapping hurts the positions most, so they are in the sketchpad. This crossover rules out the idea that one secondary task is just harder: then it would hurt both memory tasks.
m3.src: [CORE][LO B5] dual-task logic and double dissociation; E&K pp. 215-219

m3.q:
Miyake and Friedman (2012) split each executive function into a part that all three share and a part that is unique to it. Judge these statements.
I. The shared part is the ability to actively maintain task goals and use them to bias lower-level processing.
II. After the shared part was taken out, no unique variance was left for shifting.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
m3.spot: Unity and diversity: which function has nothing of its own?
m3.why: Statement I is the definition of the common executive factor (Miyake & Friedman, 2012). Statement II names the wrong function: it was inhibition that had no unique variance left (Friedman et al., 2008); shifting and updating kept a unique part. So the executive shows unity (a shared core) and diversity (specific skills).
m3.src: [LO B4][CORE] Miyake & Friedman (2012); Friedman et al. (2008); E&K p. 221

m3.q: On four Brown/Peterson trials a participant is asked to remember three animal names each time, and recall gets worse from trial to trial. On trial 5 she gets three digits instead, and recall is almost back to the level of trial 1. What is this?
o: Release from proactive interference
Retroactive interference
The recency effect
Chunking of the digits into larger units
m3.spot: Performance drops over trials, then jumps back after a switch of category.
m3.why: Earlier animal names interfere with new ones: proactive interference. Switching to a different category (digits) removes most of that interference, so recall recovers: release from proactive interference. Retroactive interference is new material spoiling old memories; the recency effect is about list position; chunking is grouping items into units.

m3.q: Which of these statements about the phonological loop is NOT correct?
o: Spoken words must pass through the articulatory control process before they enter the phonological store
Written words must be converted into a speech-based code before they enter the phonological store
Articulatory suppression occupies the articulatory control process
Sounds in the phonological store fade within about two seconds unless they are rehearsed
m3.spot: Heard words or read words: which ones need the inner voice to get in?
m3.why: Spoken words enter the phonological store directly. It is written words that must first be ‘said’ by the articulatory control process to get in (Baddeley, 1990). That is why articulatory suppression removes the word-length effect for written words. The other statements are correct.
